Votes are still being counted, but the 2026 midterms can be safely described
as a crushing Democratic Party victory. They flipped Senate seats in Kansas,
Maine, Ohio, Iowa, and North Carolina - the latter by a 20-point margin.
Democrats flipped the Senate seat in _South Carolina_ - a state where
Republicans had won the last Senate election by _more than 25 points_ - by
about 4 points.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico curb-stomped Ken Paxton in the Senate race
by 12 points, and Dems won the governor's race, may take the Texas House, and
came close to taking the Texas Senate. The Senate elections in Mississippi -
_Mississippi_ , for Pete's sake - and Alaska remain too close to call, but in
the former, Democrat Scott Colom is ahead by a whisker, while his co-partisan
Mary Peltola is ahead by a slightly wider margin at time of writing.

So in the Senate, Democrats will have between 54 and 56 seats in 2027. In the
House, many races have not been called yet (particularly in California, which
always takes forever to count), but it will probably be around 250 seats or
more.

These are huge majorities, particularly in our hyper-polarized times. That
large margin has implications for the upcoming Democratic Congress. On the one
hand, it won't be possible for any small caucus, whether it is the "Squad" on
the left (which has five new
[lawmakers](https://newrepublic.com/post/217572/dsa-candidates-won-election)
from the Democratic Socialists of America ) or centrist sellouts like Senator
John Fetterman (D-Pa.) on the right, to hold the whole party agenda hostage.

On the other hand, with such a sweeping victory, the Democratic leadership
will face strong expectations for action against a wildly corrupt and criminal
Trump administration, and a caucus that is not at all unified either
ideologically or tactically.
